briefs.summary: The midterms moved two markets in opposite directions. Democrats took both chambers on 3 Nov; traders read it as both a cheaper path to a US–Iran deal and a costlier one for AI data centres. Brent fell about 16% to US$98, its steepest week since 2020, with no deal signed and US diesel stocks at a 23-year low. On 5 Nov chips had their worst day since COVID (SOX −12%, AMD −17% despite a strong guide), and SMH ended the week 11% lower. Money hid in staples (XLP +0.7%) and SIA rose on cheaper fuel. A strong US jobs report lifted December hike odds to ~77%, yet the 10y fell. In SG, the STI dropped 3.7% to 5,179, through support, as DBS and UOB missed and UOB cut its NIM guide. Sheng Siong and Wilmar hit 52-week lows, and Cat A COE hit a record S$139,001 while Cat B held at S$132,334.
quiet: Macro (SG): no MAS action or new official data this week; USD/SGD 1.282 vs 1.278. Mid-December MOM report and late-November CPI are the next datapoints.

sections.headline: Chips have their worst day since COVID on 5 Nov (SOX −12%, AMD −17%) after the Democratic midterm sweep raises AI-regulation fears; AMD's own guide was strong, so this was positioning and policy, not fundamentals

what_happened.text: 5 Nov: S&P 500 −4.4%, Nasdaq Composite −5.5% (into correction), Nasdaq-100 −6.3% (~US$2.3tn), PHLX Semiconductor −12%. Coverage tied the sell-off to the Democrats winning both chambers on 3 Nov and the risk of tighter AI and data-centre rules; Nomura's McElligott called it hedge funds locking in 2026 gains rather than a change in fundamentals.

AMD (3 Nov): Q3 revenue US$13.4bn (+45%), data centre US$8.5bn (nearly doubled), Q4 guide ~US$17bn ±3%, 2027 revenue growth 'more than 80%'. Free cash flow fell to US$554m from US$1.9bn on inventory and capacity spend. Stock rose 1% on 4 Nov, then fell 17.3% on 5 Nov; down 37% from its 6 Oct peak.

Week (2–6 Nov): Nasdaq −3.4%, S&P −2.7%; SOX −12%+, Micron ~−22%, Nvidia ~−9%. Reports (unverified) that the incoming Texas governor proposed pausing new data-centre projects and that Ohio towns restricted facilities. Friday was a relief day (Nasdaq +1.7%) after strong payrolls.

sections.first_order: The AI trade lost its political cover in one session. SMH fell 11% on the week to 463.96, through last week's 511.63 'weaker' line. The fundamentals reported this week (AMD's guide) did not deteriorate; what changed is the expected cost and speed of the data-centre build-out if a Democratic Congress and states restrict permits and power hook-ups. Last week's financing worry (Alphabet and Amazon funding capex with debt and equity) is still unresolved, so two risks now sit on the same names.

second_order.effect: A slower US permitting path could push hyperscaler capacity to Asia (supportive for Keppel's 50 MW SG award and Keppel DC REIT), but a capex cut would hit everyone. AJBU (Keppel DC REIT) held up at 2.17.
US data-centre power demand was the bull case for gencos; regulation risk on new sites trims that, while Sembcorp/Keppel's SG power books are driven by local contracts.

Dr Wealth flags AI-financing exposure among the reasons bank shares fell in results week; a disorderly unwind would show first in wealth-management and trading income, which already fell sharply at DBS.
Money rotated into defensives again: XLP +0.7% on a week the S&P fell 2.7%.

evidence: SMH 463.96, −11.2% on the week, below last week's 511.63 trigger; 20-day low 445.59.
SOX −12% on 5 Nov; Nasdaq Composite in correction.
AMD guide strong (Q4 ~US$17bn, 2027 >80% growth) but free cash flow down 71% y/y on capacity spend.
Democrats control both chambers from January; reported state-level data-centre pauses (unverified).
No hyperscaler capex cut announced this week; no price-per-token or GPU-hour data found for the week.
consensus: Strategists frame the drop as positioning and profit-taking, not fundamentals.
Commentators expect tighter AI and data-centre rules under a Democratic Congress.
Nvidia's late-November results are widely seen as the next test of AI demand.
sections.flip_if: Bullish if Nvidia's late-November results guide above consensus with no hyperscaler deferrals, the incoming Congress signals permitting rather than restriction, and SMH recovers above ~522 (last week's close). Stronger bearish if SMH closes below 445.59 (20-day low), a hyperscaler cuts its 2027 capex plan, or states formally pause data-centre approvals.

sections.headline: STI falls 3.7% to 5,179, breaking last week's 5,365 support; DBS and UOB miss on trading income and margins, UOB cuts its NIM guide to below 1.75%, OCBC beats

what_happened.text: DBS 3Q26: net profit S$2.81bn (−5% y/y, −9% q/q; consensus ~S$2.95bn). NIM 1.87% (−9bp y/y, flat q/q). Markets trading income −65% y/y to S$152m. Fees +6%, wealth fees +9%. Specific allowances 17bp; NPL 0.9%. Dividend 66c + 15c capital return (ex 13 Nov). MAS cut DBS's operational-risk multiplier to 1.5x from 1.8x on 4 Nov.

UOB 3Q26 (4 Nov): net profit S$1.25bn (−15% q/q), below a S$1.38bn poll. NIM 1.68% vs 1.74% in 2Q; CFO said FY26 NIM will likely fall below the 1.75–1.80% guide. Record fees S$733m (+19%). NPL 1.5%, Greater China NPL 5.0%. Shares −5% to S$38.44, lowest close since June; 2027 credit-cost guide 25–30bp.
OCBC 3Q26 (6 Nov): net profit S$2.04bn (+3% y/y), above ~S$2.01bn consensus. 9M NIM 1.71% (−22bp). Fees S$735m; credit costs 6bp; NPL 0.8%. Trading income −33% q/q on Great Eastern bond marks.
Dr Wealth summary: all three banks fell in results week on margin and deposit-cost worries, higher global yields, rate uncertainty and AI-financing exposure.

sections.first_order: Last week's bearish trigger fired: the STI closed at 5,179.17, below 5,365, and UOB reported NIM below 1.8%. Banks are about 40% of the index, and two of three missed on the same two lines: margins compressing faster than guided and trading income collapsing in volatile markets. Fee growth and clean credit (DBS 17bp, OCBC 6bp) are the offsets. The REITs on the watchlist held up (CICT +2.6%, CLAR +2.3%, PLife +0.8%) as yields stayed below 4.9%.

second_order.effect: Falling bank shares and a risk-off tape have not hurt REITs; they benefit if MAS and SORA stay low. A US hike in December is the risk to that.
Volatility lifts SGX trading volumes and derivatives revenue; S68 rose 1.4% on the week.
Banks guiding lower NIM and higher credit costs (UOB 25–30bp in 2027) may tighten consumer and auto lending at the margin, one channel to the dealer-pullback gate.
Record fees at UOB and OCBC and +9% at DBS show flows still coming to SG; a prolonged equity drawdown would slow them.

evidence: STI 5,179.17, −3.7% on the week, below 5,365 support; 20-day low 5,138.75.
UOB NIM 1.68% and guide cut below 1.75–1.80%; DBS NIM 1.87% (−9bp y/y); OCBC 9M NIM 1.71% (−22bp).
DBS trading income −65% y/y; OCBC trading −33% q/q.
Credit quality stable: DBS NPL 0.9%, OCBC 0.8%, UOB 1.5% (Greater China 5.0%).
UOB −10.9% on the week to 36.88; DBS −4.7% to 69.72; OCBC −5.3% to 27.73.
CLAR 2.26 is below Norman's 2.50–2.60 band; UOB 36.88 is ~12% above his 31–33 band; all others are above their bands.
consensus: Analysts see NIM compression as largely priced and dividends as the support for bank shares.
Commentary calls OCBC the relative winner on credit costs and guidance.
Citi downgraded OCBC in October on valuation and NIM (cited by Dr Wealth).
sections.flip_if: Back to mixed if the STI retakes 5,365 and holds while banks trade ex-dividend without new lows (DBS ex 13 Nov). Stronger bearish if the STI closes below 5,138.75 (20-day low), UOB breaks 36.54, or a December Fed hike lifts SORA and compresses REIT yields.

sections.headline: Cat A hits a record S$139,001 while Cat B edges up 0.3% to S$132,334 on the larger quota; Cat B bids/quota eases to 1.21x

what_happened.text: 4 Nov (1st Nov round): Cat A S$139,001 (+S$6,997, record; previous high S$133,009), Cat B S$132,334 (+S$433), Cat C S$92,000, Cat D S$10,689, Cat E S$135,998 (+S$208). Bids/quota: A 2,018/1,189, B 1,163/959, E 506/287. Next round 16–18 Nov.

Dealers expect Cat A to pass S$140K on year-end targets and the end of the EV Early Adoption Incentive (S$7,500 ARF rebate) on 31 Dec. One dealer cited Car Expo and 'the loan clampdown by LTA' (no detail given). Cat B PQP S$131,819 for November.

sections.first_order: The 3.3% larger Cat B quota did its job only partly: Cat B was flat (+0.3%) and bids per certificate fell to 1.21x from ~1.3x, while unmet demand moved to Cat A (1.70x, record premium). Cat B stayed inside last week's band (above S$130,100, below S$135,001), so neither 'rising' nor 'falling' trigger fired. Cat B at S$132K is S$52K above the S$80K thesis level.

second_order.effect: Mass-market EV demand pulled ahead of the 31 Dec incentive end is landing in Cat A; dealers clear orders but face a post-January air pocket.
A reported LTA loan clampdown (unverified) and banks guiding higher 2027 credit costs both cut against financing-driven PHV bidding.
PQP for Cat B rises to S$131,819, keeping renewal costs and used-car prices high.

evidence: Cat B S$132,334 (+0.3%), bids/quota 1.21x vs ~1.3x before.
Cat A S$139,001 record; bids/quota 1.70x; Cat A above Cat B for a fifth time this year.
EEAI rebate ends 31 Dec 2026, so December rounds carry the last pull-forward.
Thesis gates: COE level gate still missed (Cat B > S$110K); retrenchment gate moved last week; dealer-pullback gate has only anecdotal evidence (loan clampdown remark).
consensus: Dealers expect Cat A above S$140K into year-end.
Commentary expects a post-incentive dip in early 2027 rounds.
PHV fleet and easy-financing demand is widely cited as keeping Cat B high.
sections.flip_if: Premiums rising: Cat B clears above S$135,001 on 18 Nov or 7 Dec, or bids/quota climbs back above 1.3x. Premiums falling: Cat B below ~S$130,100 with bids/quota toward 1.1x, LTA confirms tighter car-loan rules, or January rounds show the post-incentive drop. Toward S$80K: needs the mid-December MOM report to confirm rising retrenchments plus a larger February–April quota.

sections.headline: Brent falls about 16% on the week to US$98 on US–Iran deal bets after the midterms; no deal is signed and physical data stay tight, but the market has stopped paying a war premium

what_happened.text: Brent fell ~16% and WTI ~13% on the week, the steepest weekly drop since 2020. Drivers cited: Republican midterm losses read as de-escalation, Iran studying Qatari proposals. JPMorgan puts the global surplus at 1.4 mb/d in October; Goldman calls the market balanced. EIA: US distillate stocks 99.3 mb, lowest since 2003; refinery utilisation 94.5%.

An unnamed senior Iranian official said Hormuz could reopen within two days if the US lifts oil sanctions and frees assets; VP Vance said the sides had 'made some progress'. Brent settled US$94.62 on 4 Nov (−8.7%) then US$98.29 on 5 Nov. The Jan/Dec 2027 Brent spread narrowed to ~US$15 from ~US$19. No agreement signed.

IRGC claimed more tankers hit mines (not confirmed by JMIC, CENTCOM or UKMTO); a Greek-operated tanker was struck off Qatar with one crew killed. Kpler preliminary data put Hormuz flows near 14 mb/d (~82% of pre-war). Eurasia Group puts deal odds at 10%.

sections.first_order: Last week's bullish read flipped on its own trigger: XLE closed at 61.62, below 66.29, and the majors lost 10–12% (XOM 165.87, SHEL 99.09). The move is driven by expectations, not by barrels: no deal exists, Hormuz flows are still ~18% below normal and US diesel stocks are at a 23-year low. But the backwardation is flattening, the demand loss (~3.3 mb/d since the war began, per reports) is large, and banks now model a surplus. The market will not pay up for supply risk until talks break.

second_order.effect: Jet fuel follows crude down; SIA (C6L) rose 3.9% on the week to 6.95. Lower fuel costs lag fares, so margins widen first.
The Oct–Dec fuel window that sets Q1 2027 tariffs now averages lower than the US$105–117 range of October; a smaller Q1 rise is likely if Brent holds near US$100.
Cheaper diesel and bunker fuel ease freight and packaging costs with a 1–2 quarter lag; supports staples margins.
Diesel margins fell in Europe this week but stocks remain tight; refining earnings stay elevated even with lower crude.

evidence: Brent 98.32 (−16% w/w), WTI 90.83 (−13%); XLE 61.62 (−12%), below last week's 66.29 trigger.
Brent Jan/Dec 2027 spread narrowed to ~US$15 from ~US$19.
JPMorgan surplus estimate 1.4 mb/d (Oct); Goldman 'broadly balanced'.
Against: US distillate stocks lowest since 2003; Hormuz flows ~82% of pre-war; no signed deal; ship attacks continuing.
No OPEC+ news this week; next meeting 29 Nov.
consensus: Traders price a US–Iran deal; Eurasia Group puts the odds at only 10%.
Commentary expects Trump to choose between new strikes, pressure or negotiation soon.
sections.flip_if: Bullish again if talks collapse or US strikes resume (reports of new strikes on 7 Nov are unconfirmed), Hormuz flows fall back, or Brent retakes ~US$105 with XLE back above 66. Stronger bearish if a deal is signed and PortWatch/Kpler show transits recovering above 90% of pre-war, or OPEC+ adds barrels on 29 Nov; Brent below US$93.40 would confirm.

sections.headline: Brent's drop takes pressure off the Q1 2027 tariff; Keppel's core profit grows ~15% in Q3 with S$615m of new connectivity contracts, yet Keppel and Sembcorp both fall with the market

what_happened.text: Keppel 3Q/9M update (3 Nov): core 'New Keppel' 9M net profit up >20% (Q3 ~15%); connectivity solutions revenue >S$900m for 9M, EBITDA +110%; S$615m of new contracts; 50 MW of SG data-centre capacity awarded; appointed aggregator for 120 MW of biomethane imports. Group 9M net profit −40% on non-core impairments.

Asian spot LNG for December averaged US$31.40/MMBtu in the week to 6 Nov, down from US$32.50 (highest since 2022); TTF fell ~17% to ~€86/MWh. Qatar's force majeure is extended to at least end-December.
IEA (3 Nov, via Discovery Alert): more than 60 bcm of Qatari and UAE LNG loadings lost Mar–Oct; 2026 global LNG output seen down ~3%, the steepest fall on record.

sections.first_order: SG's tariff is set off a quarterly fuel window, and roughly half of the Oct–Dec window is now behind us at prices in the US$95–117 range. If Brent stays near US$100, the Q1 2027 increase from 28.59 c/kWh is smaller than October implied. LNG has not followed oil down much (JKM still ~US$31), which matters more for SG's gas-fired gencos. Keppel's results confirm the data-centre power and connectivity story, but the stock still fell 6.3% to a 52-week low of 9.30 intraday.

second_order.effect: A smaller Q1 tariff rise lowers the energy line in CPI and business costs.
Power is a top cost line for chilled retail; a smaller tariff rise eases the squeeze Sheng Siong flagged.
Lower fuel pass-through compresses retail tariff revenue, but merchant spreads depend on LNG, which is still near 4-year highs.
Keppel's 50 MW award and biomethane role position it to supply power to SG data centres if US permitting slows.

evidence: Keppel core profit +~15% in Q3; connectivity EBITDA +110% 9M; S$615m new contracts.
Asian spot LNG US$31.40 vs US$32.50; Qatar force majeure through at least December.
Current SP tariff 28.59 c/kWh (Q4 2026); Q1 2027 tariff due end-December.
consensus: Analysts expect the Q1 2027 tariff to rise, by less than feared if oil stays near US$100.
Keppel is broadly seen as a data-centre and infrastructure play rather than an oil-and-gas name.

levels.name: Asian spot LNG (US$/MMBtu, Dec delivery, weekly avg)

sections.flip_if: Bullish for SG gencos if data-centre power contracts are announced or Sembcorp retakes ~6.17 (20-day high). Bearish if LNG stays above US$30 while oil-linked tariffs fall (margin squeeze), or Keppel breaks 9.30. Brent below ~US$95 into mid-December would cap the Q1 tariff rise further.

sections.headline: Staples hold as the market falls 2.7% (XLP +0.7%, Costco +4%); the FAO index eases 1.2% in October but sugar jumps 6.6% and vegetable oils stay near three-year highs

what_happened.text: FAO Food Price Index (6 Nov): October 133.9, −1.2% m/m, +5.9% y/y. Cereals −4.5%, dairy −1.1%, meat −1.2%; vegetable oils +0.3% to 199.2 (soybean oil highest since late 2022 on biofuel demand); sugar +6.6% to 121.3, highest since Dec 2024.
US week (2–6 Nov): S&P 500 −2.7%, Nasdaq −3.4% while defensives held; a strong payrolls report (+165k, wages +0.4% m/m) supports consumer spending.

sections.first_order: The rotation into staples held through the 5 Nov crash: XLP closed at 90.08, +0.7% on the week, near its 93.40 high; PG +2.4%, COST +4.1%, UL +1.1%. Input costs are mixed: grains and dairy are easing and crude fell 16%, but sugar and vegetable oils, which matter for snacks, beverages and personal care, are rising. Wage growth of 3.1% y/y supports volumes.

second_order.effect: Sugar +29% y/y and soybean oil at a 3-year high pressure Nestlé, Unilever and beverage makers' gross margins.
Lower fuel and grain costs plus wage growth favour volume-led retailers; Walmart reports mid-November.
Soybean oil strength lifts competing vegetable oils' prices, but Wilmar's issue is crush margins, not oil prices.

evidence: XLP 90.08 (+0.7%) vs S&P 500 −2.7% on the week.
FAO index 133.9 (−1.2% m/m); sugar +6.6% m/m, veg oils 199.2.
Brent −16% w/w eases freight and packaging.
US average hourly earnings +3.1% y/y.
consensus: Investors treat staples as the place to hide from the AI unwind.
Analysts expect Walmart to keep taking share from lower-income and higher-income shoppers alike.
sections.flip_if: Bearish if tech stabilises and the rotation reverses (XLP below ~86), or if sugar and veg-oil gains lead to margin-guide cuts. Stronger bullish if XLP breaks 93.40 and Walmart's mid-November results show volume gains.

sections.headline: Sheng Siong falls 12% on the week to a 52-week low of 2.35 as same-store sales shrink; Wilmar breaks below 3.00 to a new 52-week low

what_happened.text: Sheng Siong Q3: revenue +6.2% but same-store sales shrank (high base from government vouchers), with labour costs rising and a maturing footprint of 92 stores; shares fell ~14% over two days.
Sheng Siong Q3 net profit S$44.6m (+1.9% y/y); shares fell as much as 8.6% on Monday after a 4.6% drop on Friday 30 Oct.

sections.first_order: Last week's bearish read strengthened. Sheng Siong (2.35, −12%) and Wilmar (2.97, through the 3.00 level flagged last week) both made 52-week lows. The new fact is that Sheng Siong's existing stores are shrinking, which is a demand signal on top of the cost squeeze. DFI Retail (3.73, +6.9%) and Thai Beverage (0.435, +2.4%) went the other way, so this is company-specific more than sector-wide.

second_order.effect: Shrinking same-store sales at a value grocer hint at stretched households; heartland mall tenants' sales are the next thing to watch.
Easing FAO grains and lower fuel argue for food inflation peaking; sugar and edible oils argue against.
Sheng Siong citing labour costs while retrenchments rise shows wage pressure in lower-paid service jobs persists despite a softer job market.

evidence: Sheng Siong same-store sales shrank; profit +1.9%.
consensus: Analysts attribute Sheng Siong's slowdown mainly to the voucher base effect, expected to fade in 2027.
Wilmar is seen as cheap but lacks a catalyst until crush margins recover.
sections.flip_if: Bullish if Sheng Siong holds 2.32 and October retail sales (mid-December) show supermarket volumes stabilising, or the Q1 tariff comes in flat. Stronger bearish if October food CPI (late November) tops 2.5% while retailers' same-store sales keep shrinking, or Wilmar breaks 2.91.

sections.headline: Payrolls beat (+165k vs ~60k expected, unemployment 4.1%, wages +0.4%) and lift December hike odds to ~77%, but the 10y ends lower at 4.86% as the oil collapse and equity rout pull the other way

what_happened.text: October payrolls +165k (consensus ~59–65k); unemployment 4.1% (from 4.2%); average hourly earnings +0.4% m/m, +3.1% y/y; Aug and Sep revised up ~84k combined. CME FedWatch: 25bp December hike odds ~77%. FOMC meets 8–9 Dec; fed funds 3.75–4.00%.
After the report: 2y +6bp to 4.52%, 10y +3bp to 4.87%, 30y 5.27%; dollar index +0.7% to 102.22.
Democrats won both chambers on 3 Nov; Bank of England raised rates 25bp to 4% (8–1).

sections.first_order: Half of last week's bearish-bond trigger fired (hot payrolls), the other half did not (10y at 4.86%, well below 5.15%). The two big forces offset: a hot labour market and a Fed likely to hike in December push yields up; a 16% oil drop and a tech crash push inflation expectations and growth down. TLT finished flat at 81.92. October CPI on 10 Nov decides which wins.

second_order.effect: A December hike with strong jobs supports the dollar (DXY +0.7% Friday), pressuring SGD at the margin.
A Fed hike lifts SORA and REIT funding costs; falling oil limits how far long yields rise.
Mortgage rates stay high with the 10y near 4.9%; strong wages offset.

evidence: Payrolls +165k; unemployment 4.1%; AHE +3.1% y/y.
December hike odds ~77% (from ~70%).
10y 4.86% (from 4.93% a week ago); TLT 81.92 (flat).
Brent −16% w/w lowers headline inflation into Q1.
Democratic Congress from January: fiscal path uncertain.
consensus: Markets expect a December hike; commentary calls it 'sealed' after payrolls.
Many strategists expect the AI rout to tighten financial conditions enough to make it the last hike.
sections.flip_if: Bullish for bonds if October CPI (10 Nov) is soft, December hike odds fall below ~50%, and the 10y breaks 4.81% (20-day low). Bearish if CPI runs hot, the 10y retakes 5.15%, or the new Congress signals large fiscal expansion.

briefs.summary: The AI worry moved from spending to how it is paid for. Alphabet burned US$9.1bn of cash in a second straight quarter and covered it with US$28.7bn of bonds and US$12.4bn of new shares. Amazon's trailing cash flow is −US$42bn. Microsoft is the one large spender funding capex from its own cash. On Friday, Intel's guide sent chips down 7.2% and the Nasdaq had its worst month since March 2025. Money went to staples (up more than 10% in October; Unilever raised its volume guide) and energy (XLE at a 52-week high; Shell and Exxon raised buybacks on US$33–42/bbl refining margins), while OPEC+ held and Brent ended October at US$113. US yields fell even as PCE (3.6%) and two hawkish Fed dissents argued for a hike. In SG, retrenchments hit their highest since 2020, the STI is 0.2% above support going into DBS/OCBC results (5–6 Nov), Wilmar and Sheng Siong both flagged input-cost squeezes, and LTA added 3.3% more Cat B COEs for the 2–4 Nov round.

sections.headline: Alphabet burns cash for a second quarter and turns to debt and new shares; Intel's guide sinks chips 7% on Friday; Microsoft is the one hyperscaler that funds capex from cash

what_happened.text: Alphabet Q3 (28 Oct): revenue US$127.6bn (+25%), Google Cloud US$30.7bn (+103%), capex US$51.3bn (Q2: US$44.9bn). Free cash flow was −US$9.1bn, its second negative quarter in a row. It raised US$28.7bn of senior unsecured debt and US$12.4bn from at-the-market share sales. 2026 capex guide (up to US$205bn) unchanged; 2027 flagged as a 'significant increase' with no number. GOOGL fell ~11% on 29 Oct.

Microsoft Q1 FY27 (28 Oct): revenue US$92.3bn (+19%), Azure +48% against 44% expected, capex US$45.2bn with more than US$50bn guided for next quarter. Free cash flow was +US$18.6bn and is guided positive for the full year. Commercial RPO is US$677bn (+73%).

Amazon Q3 (29 Oct): revenue US$201.9bn (+12%), slightly below the ~US$202.3bn consensus. AWS US$46.0bn (+39%) with US$17.8bn operating income. 2026 capex is ~US$220bn with more next year. Trailing-12-month free cash flow is −US$42.4bn (a year ago: +US$14.7bn). Jassy guided AWS growth above 40% in 2027 and 2028.

Intel (29 Oct): Q3 revenue US$16.51bn (+21%), adjusted EPS US$0.52, both beats. But the Q4 revenue guide of US$15–16bn missed the ~US$17.07bn consensus. INTC fell ~29% on 30 Oct (close US$65.76, from US$86.96 a week earlier).

Fri 30 Oct: Philadelphia Semiconductor Index −7.2% (largest fall since 5 Jun), SOXX −8%+, NVDA −4.2%, Nasdaq Composite −2.86% to 25,437, S&P 500 −1.82% to 7,580. Applied Materials fell ~5% and Lam ~5.5%. The Nasdaq lost 5.3% in October, its worst month since March 2025.
Over the week, the Magnificent 7 fell 3.2% while the equal-weight S&P 500 rose 0.8%, showing money rotating out of the largest tech names rather than leaving equities.

sections.first_order: Demand for AI compute still looks strong: Azure +48%, AWS +39%, Google Cloud +103%, and Microsoft's backlog is US$677bn. What changed is how the spending gets paid for. Two of the four largest spenders (Meta, Alphabet) now have negative quarterly free cash flow, and Amazon's trailing free cash flow is deeply negative. Alphabet is paying for capex with new bonds and new shares. The market has stopped rewarding capex announcements. It now marks down whichever companies cannot fund their capex from their own cash.

second_order.sector: Semiconductors and equipment (NVDA, AMD, AMAT, LRCX)
second_order.effect: Chips moved on the funding worry even though suppliers' order books are full (Lam guided its December quarter up last week). If hyperscalers push equity and debt markets for funding, investors assume capex growth slows in 2027–28, and suppliers are priced for that before it shows up in their orders.
Alphabet's US$28.7bn deal adds to Meta's financing. A larger stream of hyperscaler bond issuance widens tech credit spreads and competes with other issuers for buyers.
If even Alphabet has to raise outside money, weaker borrowers sit further back in the queue. Their cost of capital stays punitive.

second_order.sector: Power and data-centre infrastructure (Keppel DC, Sembcorp, utilities)
second_order.effect: Capex is still rising: MSFT guides more than US$50bn next quarter and Amazon expects more in 2027. Contracted power demand for data centres is intact for now, even as chip stocks reprice.
Money leaving tech went to defensives: staples rose more than 10% in October and the equal-weight S&P was up this week. Those flows hold up as long as AI doubts persist.

evidence: GOOGL Q3 free cash flow −US$9.1bn (second negative quarter), funded by US$28.7bn of debt and US$12.4bn of ATM equity. This meets last week's bearish trigger: a second hyperscaler with negative free cash flow alongside new debt or equity funding.
AMZN trailing-12-month free cash flow −US$42.4bn against 2026 capex of ~US$220bn.
MSFT free cash flow +US$18.6bn and guided positive for FY27; Azure +48%. It is the exception.
SOX −7.2% on 30 Oct. SMH closed at 522.49, just above last week's 520.53 bear-confirmation level, after trading down to 511.63 intraday.
INTC Q4 revenue guide of US$15–16bn against ~US$17.07bn consensus; stock −29%.
No new H100 rental-index print was verified this week. Last week's reading was US$3.71/GPU-hr and rising.
consensus: JPMorgan's trading desk says doubts about whether AI will pay off are deepening the rotation out of tech.
Raymond James says the fundamentals for AI-capex beneficiaries are intact and negative free cash flow is manageable.
Commentators widely read Microsoft as the winner because it funds capex from cash.
sections.flip_if: Bullish if Nvidia's late-November results guide above consensus with no sign of hyperscaler order deferrals, if the H100 rental index keeps rising, and SMH closes back above ~571. Weaker if SMH closes below 511.63, a hyperscaler cuts its 2027 capex plan, or another large AI-linked bond deal prices wide.

sections.headline: STI slides 0.8% to 5,376.74, just above its 5,365 support, as retrenchments hit a post-2020 high; CICT's update shows positive reversions and cheaper debt

what_happened.text: CICT 3Q 2026 (29 Oct): net property income S$334.9m (+13.8% y/y). 9M rent reversions +7.1% office and +4.6% retail. Occupancy 96.1%. Average cost of debt down to 2.8% from 2.9%. Gearing up to 39.7% from 37.4% after the Paragon acquisition.

MOM advance release (30 Oct): Q3 retrenchments 4,800, the highest since 2020 (Q2: ~4,620). Resident unemployment rose to 3.0% and citizen unemployment to 3.1% in September. Employment grew 27,700. MOM flagged 'emerging weaknesses' that warrant monitoring.
Singapore shares fell on 30 Oct; MT Newswires tied the move to the rising-unemployment data. STI closed the week at 5,376.74 (prior week 5,422.16), after an intraday low of 5,365.13.
Bank Q3 results are next: DBS on 5 Nov, OCBC on 6 Nov, UOB expected the week after. DBS's NIM was 1.87% in 2Q26 (−18bp); 1.8% is the line analysts watch.

sections.first_order: SG stocks are caught between two forces. REIT fundamentals are improving: positive reversions plus a falling cost of debt is the combination that supports DPU. The labour market and bank margins are weakening. The STI sits right on its October support going into bank results, and banks are about 40% of the index.

second_order.effect: CICT's cost of debt fell 10bp in a quarter and the US 10y slipped to 4.93%. If that continues, it is the first real relief on REIT financing costs, though higher gearing after Paragon limits headroom.
Lower SORA squeezes NIM. Rising retrenchments raise the risk of higher credit costs. Fee and wealth income has to carry results on 5–6 Nov.
Resident unemployment of 3.0% and more firms expecting to retrench point to softer discretionary spending. The Sheng Siong section shows the cost side.
Volatility helps trading volumes, but S68 still fell 2.7% on the week, so the market isn't paying for that yet.

evidence: STI 5,376.74, 0.2% above the 5,365 support zone; ES3 5.45.
CICT: reversions +7.1%/+4.6%, cost of debt 2.8% (−10bp q/q), gearing 39.7%.
MOM: Q3 retrenchments 4,800 (highest since 2020); resident unemployment 3.0%.
Week moves: DBS −1.8%, OCBC +1.0%, UOB −0.5%, CICT −0.9%, CLAR −0.9%, PLife −2.2%, SGX −2.7%.
consensus: Brokers see DBS/OCBC NIMs holding near 1.8% and are more cautious on UOB.
Consensus treats S-REITs as the main beneficiary once global rates turn.
sections.flip_if: Bearish if the STI closes below 5,365, or DBS/OCBC (5–6 Nov) report NIM below 1.8% or a jump in specific provisions. Bullish if banks hold NIM near 1.8% with fee growth and the STI retakes ~5,458 (this fortnight's high).

sections.headline: LTA lifts the Nov–Jan Cat B quota 3.3% to 5,707, with 959 certificates in the first round; first bids under the new quota close 4 Nov

what_happened.text: LTA (26 Oct): Nov 2026–Jan 2027 quota of 19,298 (+1.1%). Cat A unchanged at 7,134; Cat B 5,707 (+3.3% from 5,527); Cat E 1,580 (+3.7%). LTA said the quota is unaffected by its ongoing review of how cars are assigned to COE categories. The next quota announcement is in January 2027.
November round 1 quota: Cat A 1,189, Cat B 959, Cat E 287. Bidding runs 2–4 Nov, then 16–18 Nov and 7 Dec. Last result (21 Oct): Cat A S$132,004, Cat B S$131,901, Cat E S$135,790.
MOM (30 Oct): Q3 retrenchments rose to 4,800, the highest since 2020, and more firms said they expect to retrench. This is one of the demand-side gates in the S$80K thesis.

sections.first_order: Slightly more Cat B supply arrives just as the EV incentive pull-forward peaks. 959 per round is above the ~923 level flagged last week as the line for a tighter quarter. On supply alone, that removes one reason for premiums to rise. A 3% quota change is still small next to bids running about 1.3x quota, so the 2–4 Nov round is the real test.

second_order.effect: More Cat B certificates let dealers clear EV orders taken at the Car Expo. Margins depend on whether premiums hold after the incentive ends with 2026 registrations.
Higher retrenchments and resident unemployment at 3.0% raise the risk on zero-deposit, full-loan PHV purchases, the financing-driven demand behind recent bidding.
Premiums near S$132K keep PQP renewals and resale values high. A softer Cat B round would show up first in parallel-import and used-car pricing.

evidence: Cat B quota 5,707 (+3.3%); 959 per round, above last week's ~923 'tighter' line.
Cat A was unchanged and closed above Cat B for the fourth time this year, so mass-market demand is still spilling over.
Retrenchments 4,800 (highest since 2020), the first move on the retrenchment gate.
No new bidding result this week; the last Cat B result is S$131,901.
consensus: Dealers and commentators expect premiums to stay elevated into year-end on EV pull-forward and PHV fleet demand.
Commentary expects a post-incentive dip in early 2027.

Premiums falling: Cat B closes below ~S$130,100 with bids/quota toward 1.1x, or the January rounds show the post-incentive drop. Toward the S$80K thesis: needs further retrenchment rises (full MOM report mid-Dec), dealer pullback and a bigger quota in January.

sections.headline: Majors post their best quarter since 2022 on refining: Shell lifts its buyback to US$5bn and Exxon sets US$20bn; OPEC+ holds December; Brent ends October at US$113.43 (+13.6% in the month)

what_happened.text: OPEC+ (1 Nov): the seven-country group held December targets for a third month. The capacity review moves to mid-November, and the full 21-member meeting on 29 Nov sets the 2027 framework. Brent's January contract settled at US$113.43 on 30 Oct; the expired December contract finished at US$117.64.

Shell Q3 (29 Oct): net profit US$10.81bn (consensus US$10.33bn), buyback raised to US$5bn from US$3bn, refining margin US$42/bbl (nearly 4x y/y). Qatar disruption partly offset LNG Canada volumes, and Pearl GTL repairs could take about a year. TotalEnergies' adjusted profit of US$9.1bn is its highest since 2022.

Exxon Q3 (30 Oct): adjusted EPS US$4.23 (consensus US$4.12), revenue US$113.2bn (+33%), Gulf Coast refineries at 100% utilisation, dividend raised to US$1.07, US$20bn buyback. Chevron: net income US$9.9bn (US$5.06/sh), revenue +36%, US refinery utilisation 98%. US diesel is ~US$6.32/gal, +71% y/y.
JKM for December delivery was in the high US$31s/MMBtu on 23 Oct (from high US$29s). EU storage is 74.6%, 16.6% below the five-year average, with the first winter withdrawal on 20 Oct.

sections.first_order: Majors are converting the Hormuz shock into cash. Refining margins of US$33–42/bbl and refineries running near 100% mean the windfall sits mainly in downstream, not only crude. Buybacks are being raised rather than held. XLE closed at a 52-week high of 70.02. OPEC+ is holding rather than adding barrels, so the supply cushion is no bigger.

second_order.effect: Diesel and jet-fuel cracks at these levels keep fuel the biggest cost pressure. Carriers have to raise fares or cut capacity going into peak season, which weighs on travel demand at the margin.

second_order.sector: Freight, logistics and staples input costs
second_order.effect: US diesel +71% y/y feeds straight into distribution costs. Unilever is already pushing commodity-driven price increases in Home Care, and P&G flagged a US$1.4bn hit last week.

second_order.sector: Asian power and LNG importers (SG, Japan, Korea)
second_order.effect: JKM in the low US$30s and tight EU storage mean Asia is competing for LNG cargoes through winter. That sets up higher Q1 2027 tariffs in SG.
Gold fell ~3.5% to a one-year low on 30 Oct even with oil above US$110. Markets are treating oil as a growth tax rather than an inflation scare, which leaves energy equities as the main hedge.

evidence: XLE 70.02, a 52-week closing high (week +1.0%); XOM and CVX also at 52-week highs.
Shell buyback US$3bn→US$5bn; Exxon US$20bn buyback and dividend raise.
Refining margins: Shell US$42/bbl, Total US$33.2/bbl.
OPEC+ held December targets; no extra barrels.
Brent front-month (January) US$113.43. Part of the drop from last week's US$116.72 is the contract roll; the December contract expired at US$117.64.

Market chatter of a bull case at Brent US$120 and a bear case at US$106–107 for the week ahead.
Commentators widely expect the OPEC+ hold to be priced in.

sections.headline: The Oct–Dec fuel window that sets Q1 2027 tariffs runs at Brent US$105–117 and JKM in the low 30s; Keppel's integrated power EBITDA grows 7% while Sembcorp slips

what_happened.text: SP Group's Q4 2026 household tariff is 28.59 c/kWh, down 10.4%, priced off July–September fuel. Q1 2027 will be priced off October–December fuel, which has been running much higher.

Keppel 9M 2026 (29 Oct): net profit excluding the non-core portfolio rose more than 20%. Integrated power EBITDA +7%, helped by the start of commercial operations at the Keppel Sakra Cogen plant. The data-centre/connectivity business contributed to growth. Asset monetisation is S$3.7bn, above the S$2–3bn target.
JKM December delivery was in the high US$31s/MMBtu on 23 Oct, up about US$2 on the week.
Sheng Siong (29 Oct) named electricity, alongside labour and transport, as costs it expects to weigh on margins.

sections.first_order: For SG gencos, higher fuel costs are largely passed through to customers with a lag. Keppel's 7% power EBITDA growth shows the integrated model holding margins so far. The pain moves to households and businesses through a likely Q1 2027 tariff increase, announced around end-December.

second_order.effect: Electricity and gas are in the CPI basket. A Q1 2027 tariff increase would add to the headline print and could reverse part of the Q4 cut's drag on inflation.

second_order.sector: SG supermarkets and F&B (Sheng Siong, DFI)
second_order.effect: Refrigerated retail is power-intensive. Sheng Siong has already flagged electricity as a margin headwind.

second_order.sector: Data centres (Keppel DC REIT, Digital Core REIT)
second_order.effect: Data centres can mostly pass power costs through, and hyperscaler capex keeps contracted demand rising. Margin risk sits with operators on fixed-price contracts.

evidence: Keppel integrated power EBITDA +7% in 9M; BN4 +0.9% on the week to 10.09.
Sembcorp −2.7% to 5.85 (range 5.62–6.13 over 10 sessions).
Fuel window: Brent US$105.95–117.42 over 10 sessions; JKM high US$31s.
Q4 tariff 28.59 c/kWh (−10.4%).
consensus: Consensus expects a Q1 2027 tariff increase given the fuel-cost lag.
Brokers see Keppel's asset-light pivot as intact.

sections.headline: Unilever raises its volume guide to at least 3%, the clean volume test P&G and Nestlé only partly passed; staples rose more than 10% in October as money left tech

what_happened.text: Unilever Q3 (late Oct): underlying sales growth 5.2% (volume 2.9%, price 2.3%). FY26 volume guide raised to at least 3%; H2 sales growth ~5%; modest FY margin improvement on 20.0%. Commodity-driven price increases are stepping up in Home Care. Foods volume fell 1.1% and developed-market volume fell 1.7%.
The consumer staples sector rose more than 10% in October while the Magnificent 7 fell. XLP closed the week at 89.42, near its 52-week high of 90.38.
US diesel ~US$6.32/gal (+71% y/y, AAA), a direct distribution-cost input for consumer goods companies.

sections.first_order: Unilever grew volumes and raised prices at the same time, and still guided margins up. That met last week's bullish trigger, and the sector is being bid as a haven from tech. The split inside the result matters: Home Care and Personal Care pass costs on, while Foods and developed markets are losing volume. Pricing power is uneven.

second_order.effect: Branded goods makers pushing commodity price increases put pressure on retailers' private-label mix. Walmart (+3.0% on the week) and Costco tend to take share when shoppers trade down.
Higher oil-linked resin and packaging costs are why Home Care pricing is rising. The cost is shared along the chain, not absorbed.
Unilever Foods volume −1.1% suggests food price increases are meeting resistance. Food is the weak spot if the FAO index (6 Nov) stays high.

XLP 89.42 (+1.3% on the week), 52-week high 90.38.

Analysts generally expect P&G's commodity headwind to hit margins in FY27.

sections.headline: Wilmar's core profit drops 25% on soybean crush and feedstock costs and the stock falls to a 52-week low of 3.01; Sheng Siong grows profit only 1.8% and flags power and labour costs

what_happened.text: Wilmar 3Q 2026 (28 Oct): revenue US$21.6bn (+14%), core net profit US$267.3m (−25.2%). It cited higher raw-material and feedstock costs and weaker soybean crush margins in its China JVs. Excluding the AWL consolidation, volume fell 2.7%. Outlook: 'challenging' but core business 'resilient'.
Wilmar fell 4.9% on 29 Oct to S$3.11 on about twice its average volume, and closed the week at S$3.01, a 52-week low (prior week S$3.34).

Sheng Siong Q3 (29 Oct): revenue S$441.5m (+6.2%), net profit S$44.6m (+1.8%). Management expects labour, transport and electricity costs, plus sustained promotions, to pressure margins. The stock fell ~5% on 30 Oct to S$2.67. Maybank had downgraded it to Hold on 9 Oct.

sections.first_order: Both SG staples bellwethers show costs outrunning prices. Wilmar is caught between feedstock and soybean crush spreads. Sheng Siong's profit growth has fallen well behind its revenue growth. This is the local version of the input-cost squeeze, and unlike Unilever, neither company has shown it can raise prices to cover it.

second_order.effect: Retailers absorbing costs now (Sheng Siong's promotions) limits food inflation in the short term. Pass-through risk builds if the Q1 tariff rises.
Steady palm prices help plantations, but downstream margins are where earnings are being lost.
Rising resident unemployment plus grocery-cost pressure moves household spending toward essentials. Sheng Siong's sales benefit, but its margins don't.

evidence: Wilmar core profit −25.2%; stock at a 52-week low of 3.01 (−9.9% on the week).
Sheng Siong net profit +1.8% on revenue +6.2%; flags electricity, labour and transport costs; stock −5.3% on the week to 2.67.
Thai Beverage 0.425 (−2.3%), near its 52-week low of 0.41.

UOB KH's Wilmar target (S$3.80) predates the result.

sections.headline: Fed holds at 3.75–4.00% with two dissents in favour of a hike; PCE at 3.6% and GDP at 3.4% run hot, yet the 10y falls to 4.93% as tech sells off; December hike priced at ~70–83%

what_happened.text: FOMC (28 Oct): held at 3.75–4.00% after September's hike. The vote was 10–2, with Hammack and Cook dissenting in favour of a 25bp hike. Warsh: the target is 2% PCE with 'no soft' target. CME odds of a December hike were 82.6% after the meeting.

Q3 GDP grew at a 3.4% annualised rate. September PCE rose 0.5% m/m and 3.6% y/y; core PCE was 3.1% y/y. Over the week, the 10y fell 6bp to 4.93% and the 2y fell 9bp to 4.59%. December hike odds were ~70.7% by Friday.
Gold fell ~3.5% to its lowest in about a year on 30 Oct, and Bitcoin dropped below US$77K after a reported Binance hack.

sections.first_order: The data say hike: PCE 3.6%, GDP 3.4%, and two dissents for a hike. Bond prices say slowdown: yields fell anyway because tech sold off. The front end eased more than the long end (2y −9bp), so the market is starting to doubt the December hike even though officials lean the other way. Both forces are real, so the read on duration is split.

second_order.effect: The 10y below 4.95% gives a small amount of mortgage relief, but a December hike would cancel it.
Falling US long yields help REIT valuations. A hike would widen the gap between USD and SGD rates and pressure SGD-funded REIT spreads less than US REITs.
The DXY was flat on the week, and USD/SGD hasn't moved. With the policy-rate gap unchanged, there is little pressure on Asian currencies yet.

evidence: Fed 10–2 hold, with two dissents for a hike.
PCE 3.6% y/y, core 3.1%; Q3 GDP 3.4% annualised.
10y 4.93% (−6bp), below last week's 4.95% bullish-for-bonds line; 2y 4.59% (−9bp).
TLT 81.84 (+0.6% on the week).

Principal says the Fed has 'room to wait for more data'.
Commentators expect the 3 Nov midterms to add volatility.

sections.headline: Retrenchments reach their highest since 2020 and resident unemployment ticks up to 3.0%; MAS on hold since 14 Oct; USD/SGD unchanged at 1.278

what_happened.text: MOM advance Q3 labour data (30 Oct): retrenchments 4,800 (highest since 2020), resident unemployment 3.0% (from 2.9%), citizen unemployment 3.1%. The share of firms expecting to retrench rose to 3.1% from 2.8%, though hiring intentions also rose. The full report is due mid-December.
MAS (14 Oct) held policy after tightening in April and July. 2026 core inflation forecast narrowed to 1.5–2.0%; 2027 core and headline 1.5–2.5%.
Q3 GDP advance estimate: +5.4% y/y (Q2: 6.2%), +1.1% q/q, the softest since Q1 2025.

sections.first_order: Growth is slowing from a high base and the labour market has started to soften. Core inflation (2.0% in September) is inside MAS's forecast. Together these remove the case for MAS tightening again in January and add a small case for easing later. A higher Q1 tariff is the one input pushing the other way.

second_order.effect: Softer jobs data plus falling SORA: NIM pressure and early credit-cost risk going into 5–6 Nov results.
Retrenchments are one of the S$80K-thesis gates and have started to move. One quarter is not a trend.
A dovish MAS read caps SGD strength against the USD while the Fed leans toward hiking.

evidence: Retrenchments 4,800 (highest since 2020); resident unemployment 3.0%.
MAS on hold (14 Oct); 2026 core forecast 1.5–2.0%.
USD/SGD 1.278, unchanged on the week (10-session range 1.276–1.283).
consensus: Economists see MAS on hold in January, with some starting to price easing later in 2027.
MOM frames the labour market as softening, not deteriorating.

briefs.summary: Two stresses got worse this week. Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia hit the main Hormuz bypass, and Brent rose 6% to US$116.72, its highest settle since April. Asian LNG went above US$30. Meanwhile the AI funding worry spread from the neoclouds to the hyperscalers: Meta raised its capex floor but posted its first negative free cash flow since 2012, and chips had their worst day since June (SOX −6.7% on 22 Oct). Money moved into Treasuries (the 10y briefly closed below 5%) and staples. The costs are building underneath, though: P&G raised its commodity hit to US$1.4bn, and a December Fed hike is still about 78% priced. In SG, core inflation undershot at 2.0%, REITs bounced off their lows, and Cat B COE rose to S$131,901 as buyers rushed EV purchases ahead of the incentive cut. MSFT, GOOGL and AMZN (28–29 Oct), the FOMC (28 Oct) and the oil majors (29–30 Oct) are all in the coming week.

sections.headline: Meta raises its capex floor but posts its first cash burn since 2012; chips post their worst day since June and the hyperscaler verdict moves to 28–29 Oct

what_happened.text: Meta Q3 2026 (21 Oct): revenue US$64.6bn against US$63.31bn expected. EPS was US$3.83 against 6.67 expected, after a US$9.89bn legal charge (US$7.40 excluding it). The 2026 capex range was narrowed to US$135–145bn from US$130–145bn, which raises the floor. The Q4 revenue guide is US$73–76bn. No 2027 capex number was given; Meta said budgets are 'still in development' and it will keep investing aggressively.

Meta's Q3 free cash flow was −US$2.12bn, its first negative quarter since 2012. Capex including finance leases was US$34.9bn against US$32.8bn of operating cash flow. Meta also announced a new listed non-voting Class C share, to be paid as a one-for-one stock dividend effective 19 Jan 2027.

Thu 22 Oct: META −7.0% to US$648.85, Philadelphia Semiconductor Index −6.7% (worst day since 23 Jun), Nasdaq Composite −2.60% to 26,008.86, S&P 500 −1.21%. AMD, Intel, Sandisk and Marvell each fell more than 8%. CoreWeave fell about 10% on renewed cost-of-capital worries.
Lam Research, September quarter (21 Oct): revenue US$8.22bn (+22% q/q), GAAP operating margin 40.0%, December-quarter guide US$8.6bn ± US$0.4bn. The stock still fell 11.8% on 22 Oct.

Tesla Q3 2026 (21 Oct): revenue US$28.0bn, adjusted EPS US$0.48, quarterly capex US$4.7bn (+110% y/y). Prior 2026 guide was more than US$25bn, framed around 'superintelligence compute' and chip manufacturing. TSLA fell 3.1% on 22 Oct as investors weighed heavier 2027–28 spending plans.

CoreWeave hit a 2026 intraday low of US$59.31 on 19 Oct and closed at US$61.12, the same day Goldman upgraded it. Total debt is about US$52bn; its 9.75% 2031 bond yields 15.7%. Five-year CDS reached a record 1,194.5bp in the prior week.
Median on-demand H100 rental price, week of 19 Oct: US$3.71/GPU-hr across 40 providers, up about 10% over 4 weeks and about 25% over 12 months.
Coming up: Microsoft FQ1 2027 on Wed 28 Oct after the close; Alphabet Q3 on Wed 28 Oct (call 4:30pm ET); Amazon Q3 on Thu 29 Oct (call 5pm ET); Intel Q3 on Thu 29 Oct after the close.

sections.first_order: Demand-side data stayed firm. Meta raised its capex floor, Lam guided higher at a record margin, and GPU rental prices kept rising. The market sold the funding side instead: the first hyperscaler to report showed capex now exceeds operating cash flow and added a new equity class. Chips had their worst day since June, and CoreWeave fell again. The question has moved from 'is there demand' to 'can even the hyperscalers fund it from cash flow'. This week's losses were milder than last week's, but SMH, NVDA and QQQ all closed the week lower.

second_order.effect: With Meta's free cash flow negative, more capex has to come from debt or equity. That makes funding language in the 28–29 Oct calls as important as the capex numbers.
A fresh ~10% drop in CoreWeave and bond yields near 15–16% keep its cost of capital punitive. If hyperscalers start leaning on external funding, the market for weaker borrowers gets more crowded.

second_order.sector: Semicap and SG suppliers (LRCX, AMAT; UMS, AEM, Frencken)
second_order.effect: Lam's record 40% margin and higher December guide point to continued tool orders. Lam's large Singapore manufacturing base and local precision-parts suppliers benefit from the volume. The 11.8% fall in Lam's shares shows that sentiment, not orders, is setting prices for now.
H100 median up about 10% in 4 weeks, so compute is still scarce and the costs of AI startups and app developers keep rising.

second_order.sector: Rate-sensitive tech and DC REITs (incl. Keppel DC REIT, Digital Core REIT)
second_order.effect: The US 10-year fell about 19bp to 4.95% on 22 Oct in a flight to safety, which eases discount rates and refinancing costs for data-centre landlords. Tenant credit risk at the neoclouds is still the offset.

evidence: Meta 2026 capex guide narrowed to US$135–145bn from US$130–145bn (floor up US$5bn); Q4 revenue guide US$73–76bn (Q3 release, 21 Oct)
Against: Meta Q3 free cash flow −US$2.12bn; capex US$34.9bn exceeded operating cash flow of US$32.8bn
Lam Research: Sept-quarter revenue US$8.22bn (+22% q/q), GAAP operating margin 40.0%, December guide midpoint US$8.6bn (8-K exhibit 99.1, 21 Oct)
Tesla Q3 capex US$4.7bn (+110% y/y); 2026 guide of more than US$25bn framed around AI compute
H100 on-demand median US$3.71/hr, about +10% over 4 weeks (GPU price index, week of 19 Oct)

what_happened.text: STI closed 5,422.16 on Fri 23 Oct, +6.63 pts (+0.12%) w/w. Closing high 5,437.99 (Wed 21 Oct), closing low 5,404.02 (Tue 20 Oct). Banks rallied on Wed (OCBC +1.2%, UOB +1.4%, DBS +0.3%) and fell on Tue, Thu and Fri.

sections.headline: Cat B COE rises 1.4% to S$131,901 as the Car Expo and the end of the EV incentive pull demand forward; Cat A tops Cat B again

what_happened.text: 2nd October 2026 exercise (closed 21 Oct): Cat A S$132,004 (+2,003; 1,574 bids / 1,191 quota), Cat B S$131,901 (+1,801; 1,149 bids / 923 quota), Cat C S$92,200 (+311; 481/308), Cat D S$10,778 (−234; 611/539), Cat E S$135,790 (−1,210; 411/270). PQP: Cat A S$129,883, Cat B S$131,819. Cat A is the second-highest on record (record S$133,009 on 9 Sep).

Motorist gives Cat C as S$92,900 in its body text and table. LTA's own release was not fetched, so treat Cat C as unconfirmed between 92,200 and 92,900. Cat A closed above Cat B for the fourth time this year.

LTA urged buyers and dealers to bid prudently ahead of the Car Expo (24–25 Oct). The EV Early Adoption Incentive (45% of ARF, cap S$7,500) ends for EVs registered from 1 Jan 2027, cutting the maximum EV ARF saving from S$30,000 to S$20,000. Remaining 2026 rounds: 2–4 Nov, 16–18 Nov, 7–9 Dec, 21–23 Dec. LTA is quoted as saying 'We expect a short-term increase in COE prices' (secondary source).

LTA consultation (opened 8 Oct, closes 11:59pm 2 Nov): merge Cat A and B into one car category with an OMV-based feebate. In the 3-band option, the bottom 35% by median OMV get a S$15,000 rebate and models above the 50th percentile pay a S$15,000 surcharge. The 5-band option uses ±S$7,500/±S$15,000 steps. Options for Cat E are to remove it or restrict it to cars. Findings due H1 2027; this is not yet policy.

LTA also flagged online initial bids, a review of bidding fees and dealer pricing shown ex-COE. It rejected pay-as-you-bid because ~3 in 4 successful 2025 Cat A/B bids were within 5% of the clearing price.
No Nov 2026–Jan 2027 quota announcement found as of 25 Oct. The last one was the LTA Aug–Oct 2026 release.
September CPI: private transport inflation slowed to 7.1% y/y from 7.5% as car price increases moderated.

sections.first_order: Bullish here means premiums rising. Cat B bids exceeded quota by 24% (1,149 vs 923), and two demand pulls (the Car Expo, and EV buyers needing 2026 registration to keep the S$7,500 EEAI) point to firm or higher premiums through the four remaining 2026 rounds. The 3-month check (25 Jan 2027) lands after that deadline, though. The January 2027 rounds lose the EV pull-forward, and the Nov–Jan quota, still unannounced, is the main swing factor. Near-term pressure is up; the window to check_on is two-sided.

second_order.effect: The registration-date cut-off for the EEAI concentrates EV orders into Nov–Dec 2026 and creates an order air-pocket in Q1 2027

A S$15,000 surcharge above the 50th OMV percentile, if adopted after H1 2027, raises the cost of premium cars relative to mass-market ones. Buyers may bring forward purchases before any change, which supports Cat B bids now.
COE rises of ~1.4% per round keep private transport inflation elevated (7.1%) even as car list-price increases slow. Private transport sits in headline CPI, not core.
Premiums above S$130K plus loan-to-value caps raise the down-payment needed, which caps loan volumes even as ticket sizes stay high
Removing or restricting Cat E would end its use as a Cat B overflow channel; Cat E S$135,790 is still the highest premium of all categories

sections.headline: Brent jumps 6% to US$116.72, highest since late April, as Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia join the Hormuz attacks; talks stall

what_happened.text: Brent settled US$116.72 on Fri 23 Oct (+US$3.55 on the day, about +6% w/w, highest settle since 29 Apr); WTI US$103.27 (+3.8% on the day, +2.3% w/w). It traded around US$108–111 on 20–22 Oct before the Saudi strikes.

The Houthis hit Saudi targets, including energy infrastructure, an oil field and an airport. Aramco told staff to leave its Dhahran HQ. The US ordered non-emergency personnel out of Saudi Arabia. No lost Saudi barrels reported; Aramco says the East-West line is at its 7m b/d maximum.

Iran's IRGC claimed seven tankers hit in or near Hormuz (unverified by AP; Trump called it fabricated). UKMTO logged 32 attacks around the Arabian Peninsula in October so far, against 16 in all of September. Flow data conflict: Kpler via Bloomberg has Gulf crude flows at 24.6m b/d in the week to 18 Oct (Vortexa 18m), while IMF PortWatch logged only 4 Hormuz transits on 18 Oct against a pre-crisis 85 a day.

US–Iran: no formal talks. Iran's FM Araqchi says he has 'no trust whatsoever' in US peace aims; President Pezeshkian says talks cannot proceed while the US blockade stays. Markets are pricing possible renewed US strikes before the 3 Nov midterms.
EIA, week to 16 Oct: commercial crude −3.1mb to 412.5mb (about 3% below the 5-yr average); gasoline −3.0mb (5% below); distillates +1.7mb to 104.3mb (9% below); SPR 282.7mb; refinery runs 93.4%.

Stock releases are small so far. DOE authorised an SPR exchange of only up to 400k bbl for Phillips 66 Lake Charles; the SPR is at its lowest since 1982. Germany's EBV made the first G7-agreed release. The US eased some Russia sanctions in exchange for more Russian diesel: 2.3mb this month, possibly 7.6mb a month later.

Asian spot LNG topped US$30/MMBtu on 20 Oct, the first time since Dec 2022, after a tanker strike in the Gulf of Aden. North Asia spot was US$29.30 in the week to 16 Oct, against US$10.40 at end-February. EU storage is 74.6% full against a ~89% seasonal norm. Qatar told buyers its force majeure runs through November, and Edison's Italian cargoes are suspended to early December.
OPEC+ (7 members) held November quotas flat at 31.01m b/d on 4 Oct; it meets next on 1 Nov. The quotas are mostly moot: Saudi output was about 8m b/d in September against a 10.478m quota.
Majors' Q3 dates: Shell 29 Oct (07:00 GMT); ExxonMobil 30 Oct (05:30 CT); Chevron call 30 Oct (11:00 ET, secondary source); BP reportedly 30 Oct (secondary source, not confirmed by BP).
XLE closed US$69.33 on 23 Oct (+2.6% on the day), a new 52-week high (intraday US$69.72).

sections.first_order: The risk has spread from Hormuz to Saudi Arabia, the main bypass (East-West line to Yanbu, then past the Houthi-contested Bab al-Mandab), so the Hormuz premium now sits on top of a Saudi-infrastructure premium. Inventories are still drawing: US crude and gasoline fell, distillates are 9% below average and the SPR is at a 1982 low, so policy buffers are thin. Majors go into Q3 prints (29–30 Oct) with Brent about 6% higher than a week ago and refining margins already flagged as record. The offsets are real but smaller: Gulf flows may be recovering (Kpler), Russian diesel is coming via the sanctions waiver, and the US administration has a midterm incentive to push prices down.

second_order.effect: Jet fuel prices track gasoil, and distillates are tight (US stocks 9% below average). Brent at US$116 lifts SIA's unhedged fuel cost. Higher fuel surcharges, on top of SG's green jet-fuel levy on flights from 1 Oct, raise fares and soften price-sensitive leisure demand. Houthi strikes on a Saudi airport add to Middle East routing risk.

JKM above US$30 plus Brent-linked term LNG (Japan, and SG's Brent-indexed gas) feeds into Q1 2027 electricity tariffs in Japan, Korea and Singapore. Qatar's force majeure through November removes the winter relief valve.
Distillate stocks are 9% below the 5-yr average heading into winter, so diesel and fuel surcharges rise. Carriers pass most of it on with a lag, while shippers' (and staples') logistics costs go up.
Product inventories are tight, Kuwaiti fuel output is still impaired and Russian refineries are under drone attack, so cracks stay high. Russian diesel to the US is the main offset.
Energy-linked packaging, freight and refrigeration costs hit consumer-goods gross margins with a 1–2 quarter lag. This week's Brent jump extends the squeeze into Q1 2027 costs.
US gasoline stocks are 5% below average, so pump prices keep headline CPI elevated into the Fed decision. That keeps pressure on long-duration assets.

sections.headline: Fuel window for the Q1 2027 tariff now runs at Brent ~US$109–117 and LNG ~US$30; SG renews its Qatar LNG MOU and names three biomethane importers

what_happened.text: EDB appointed Keppel Energy, Sembcorp Utilities and Tuas Power as aggregators in a 15-year, 300MW biomethane import sandbox (23 Oct). First supply is due by end-2028, aimed at data centres and industry. DPM Gan Kim Yong announced it with S$143m for industrial decarbonisation.

Keppel's share is up to 120MW for 15 years, 'not expected to have a material impact' on current-year EPS. Its Connectivity arm was provisionally awarded 50MW of new data-centre capacity. The 3Q business update is on 29 Oct.

PM Wong and Qatar's Emir (19 Oct, Doha) welcomed renewal of the QatarEnergy–Singapore MOU on LNG and low-carbon tech 'to support stable LNG procurement'. No volumes or terms were disclosed. Qatar's force majeure still runs through November.
EMC/EMA data: monthly average USEP hit S$332.5/MWh in August 2026 (July 245.2, Feb 132.9), the latest month published. Wholesale power is far above the level implied by the Q4 household tariff cut.
Q4 2026 household tariff is 28.59 c/kWh (−10.4%). The Q1 2027 tariff is due around end-December. No new SP Group statement this week.
Sembcorp closed S$6.01 on 23 Oct (S$6.00 on 20 Oct; day range 5.88–6.04), up from S$5.93 at last brief. 52-week range S$5.22–7.20.

sections.first_order: The fuel-cost window for the Q1 2027 tariff (roughly October to mid-December forward prices) is running well above the window behind the Q4 cut: Brent US$109–117 and Asian LNG at US$29–30. A Q1 tariff increase is the likely direction; this is an inference, not an announcement. For Sembcorp and Keppel, high wholesale prices (USEP S$332/MWh in August) support merchant generation spreads, though gencos mostly pass fuel through on contracted volumes. The biomethane roles add future optionality only, with nothing material before 2028.

sections.headline: P&G and Nestlé pass the volume test and hold guidance, but P&G raises its commodity cost hit to $1.4bn and loses 150bp of gross margin

what_happened.text: P&G FY27 Q1 (22 Oct): net sales +4% to $23.3bn and organic +4%, made up of volume +2.4%, mix +1.1% and price only +0.4%. Core EPS $2.00 (+1%). Core gross margin fell 150bp, with commodities costing 140bp, offset by 120bp of productivity savings and 20bp of pricing. Organic growth guidance (1–3%) and core EPS guidance ($6.89–7.11) held; all-in sales guidance raised to 2–4% to include the Thorne acquisition.

P&G raised its after-tax FY27 commodity cost estimate from about $1.0bn (29 Jul) to about $1.4bn and doubled its interest-cost estimate. Total headwinds are now $0.79 per share (was $0.56). The slides say cost headwinds will increase over the next few quarters.
PG rose about 6% intraday on 22 Oct, its biggest gain since 2020, as investors rotated from tech into defensives. It closed at 165.59, then fell back to 161.02 on 23 Oct.

Nestlé 9M (22 Oct): Q3 organic growth 4.0%, with real internal growth (RIG) 2.8% and pricing 1.1%; 9M organic 3.7% (RIG 1.9%, pricing 1.8%). FY26 outlook kept: 3–4% organic, a higher underlying trading operating margin, and an H2 margin broadly similar to H1. Coffee pricing continues to ease.
Unilever's Q3 trading statement is on 28 Oct, not this week. The next FAO Food Price Index is due 6 Nov; September stood at 136.0, the highest since Nov 2022.
XLP closed at 88.26 on 23 Oct (+3.31% on 22 Oct, −1.92% on 23 Oct), up 0.7% on the week. WMT closed at 119.89 (16 Oct: 118.81).

sections.first_order: The volume half of the test passed: P&G volume +2.4% and Nestlé Q3 RIG +2.8%, both with guidance held. The margin half failed: P&G's gross margin fell 150bp, its cost estimate rose 40%, and it captured only 0.4% of price. Branded makers are buying volume by not passing costs on, so earnings growth is flat (P&G core EPS +1%) even as sales grow. Haven flows from the AI selloff are lifting the sector's prices more than its fundamentals.

second_order.sector: Branded household and personal care (PG, CL, KMB)
second_order.effect: Oil-linked resins, pulp and freight push up input costs, and cost guidance has been raised ($1.0bn → $1.4bn at P&G). Price increases running at only 0.4% squeeze gross margins. Either price increases come in H1 2027 and test volumes, or EPS guidance comes under pressure.
Coffee pricing is easing, so volume (RIG) does more of the work. Margins stay flat in H2, and the FAO cereals and sugar spike shows up in costs with a lag.
Branded makers are holding prices to defend volume, which supports retailers' unit sales and private-label negotiating leverage. WMT is steady near 120.
Each AI or semis selloff (SOX −6.7% on 22 Oct) pushes money into staples. That support depends on tech volatility, not on earnings.

sections.headline: SG food inflation edges up to 2.4% as core eases to 2.0%; Wilmar falls 4% on a first-ever NEA haze notice to Singapore firms

what_happened.text: September CPI (23 Oct): headline 2.2% (Aug 2.3%), core 2.0% (Aug 2.2%), food 2.4% y/y (Aug 2.3%). Electricity and gas +8.7%, private transport +7.1%. MAS/MTI expect higher energy prices to push up regional food prices, core to stay slightly elevated in coming quarters and ease from mid-2027; risks tilted up.

NEA (23 Oct) served notices under the Transboundary Haze Pollution Act (THPA) on 10 Singapore-registered companies including Wilmar, the first such use against SG firms. The notices seek documents on Singapore and Indonesian affiliates, land concession locations and fire-prevention measures.
Wilmar told SGX on 24 Oct it will comply and is preparing the documents. Under the THPA, a conviction carries fines of up to S$100k a day, capped at S$2m.
Wilmar closed at S$3.34 on 23 Oct (day range 3.31–3.37), down from about 3.48 on 15 Oct. TipRanks lists Q3 results on 28 Oct (not confirmed from an SGX filing).

Sheng Siong closed at S$2.82 on 23 Oct (−1.74%), just below last week's 2.83 support. ThaiBev closed at 0.44 (+2.35%) on about 35m shares, roughly 5–10x recent volume; no news was found to explain it. No DFI Retail news was found.

sections.first_order: Food inflation has not rolled over: it edged up to 2.4%. That meets neither half of last week's flip condition. The easing in core comes from services and retail goods, not food or utilities. For grocers this means steady nominal basket growth while utility costs (+8.7%) stay high. Wilmar has a new governance overhang just before its Q3 print.

second_order.effect: Food CPI at 2.4% lifts the value of each basket. Brent at about $117 feeds into SG electricity tariffs with a lag, keeping store operating costs high. Margins depend on passing through costs that are already showing in the 8.7% energy CPI.

second_order.sector: Wilmar / SG-listed palm planters (First Resources, Bumitama)
second_order.effect: THPA disclosure demands raise ESG and financing-cost risk and could put off ESG-screened investors. The direct fine cap of S$2m is immaterial; the risk is reputational, tied to concession disclosure.
Food (2.4%), utilities (8.7%) and private transport (7.1%) still crowd out discretionary spending even as headline inflation eases.
MAS expects energy-driven increases in regional food prices; the 6 Nov FAO print is the next input.

sections.headline: October hike odds collapse to ~7% and the 10y briefly closes below 5% on the AI selloff, but December hike is still ~78% priced and Brent is at $117

what_happened.text: Fed H.15: 10y at 5.15/5.12/5.13 on 19–21 Oct, then 4.96 on 22 Oct, the first close below 5% since 22 Sep. 2y at 4.77/4.79/4.81, then 4.65. Effective fed funds 3.88%.

The 22 Oct bond rally came with an AI selloff: Meta −7% after earnings on a plan to fund AI with non-voting stock, SOX −6.7%, Nasdaq −2.6%. CME odds of an October hike fell to 7.2% (from 27.7% a week earlier and 55.4% a month earlier); December odds eased from about 86% to about 78%.

briefs.summary: One root cause runs through the week: US long yields at their highest since 2002 (10y closed at 5.31% on 5 Oct) on top of Brent back above US$106 from Hormuz tanker attacks. The FOMC minutes show most officials want another hike, and MAS is expected to tighten again on 14 Oct. That combination triggered a bank-led 4.1% STI drop (worst day since April 2025) and pushed SG REITs to 52-week lows. It also re-ignited input-cost inflation for staples, where PepsiCo cut EPS guidance. Refiners are the clear winners: Shell's margin is up from US$24 to US$42/bbl. AI hardware demand (TSMC, Samsung) still beats forecasts despite the OpenAI revenue reset.
